title.text: Chinese Garden and Japanese Garden, Rizal Park

title_en.text: Chinese Garden and Japanese Garden, Rizal Park

tagline.text: Two gardens of international friendship, side by side in Rizal Park

location.label: Location
location.text: Central section of Rizal Park (Luneta), Ermita, Manila, on either side of the old Planetarium

children.text: Two small gardens inside Rizal Park in Manila. The Chinese Garden was built with Taiwanese support in 1966–1967, and the Japanese Garden came from Japanese government and private donations in June 1969. Ponds, pavilions, stone lanterns, a Confucius statue and a marker for the 13 Martyrs make it a calm break in a city walk.

The Chinese Garden and the Japanese Garden are two small gardens set close together inside Rizal Park (Luneta Park) in Ermita, Manila. Many travelers see only the Rizal Monument and the big lawn and walk past them, but the National Parks Development Committee (NPDC), which manages the park, gives each garden its own page, and the old National Planetarium building is described as standing between the two. They are close enough to see in one go.
Both gardens were built with foreign donations during the Marcos era. According to the NPDC, the Chinese Garden was built with Taiwanese support in
, and the Japanese Garden was handed over to the Philippines on

. So even inside the same park, the mood changes sharply: one side is Chinese, with pavilions of red pillars and green-tiled roofs, and the other is Japanese, with stone lanterns, a stone bridge and neatly shaped trees.
The gardens are small, and about
20–30 minutes

each is enough even at a slow pace. Still, sitting on a bench by a pond filters out a layer of the noise from the roads and the plaza, and the pavilions and bridges make good photo backdrops. The Chinese Garden has a Confucius statue, and the Japanese Garden has a marker honoring 13 patriots executed in 1897, so they are more than walking paths: they tell a piece of modern Philippine history.

This guide draws on the NPDC's official pages, English Wikipedia and several travel guides. Admission fees and opening hours are described differently depending on the source and can change, so it is safest to check with the park office or the latest announcements before you go.

The entrance to the Chinese Garden is described as an ornate gate carved with swirling dragons. Inside, pavilions and pagoda-like structures with red pillars and green-tiled roofs line an artificial lagoon, and the roofs and railings are decorated with mythical figures.

The lagoon is edged with irregularly shaped Antipolo stones, and trees and plants were added to create a natural-looking landscape. The garden was designed by C.Y. Shih, a Taiwanese landscaper who was 78 at the time, and he was assisted by Ernesto Villavicencio, a Filipino-Chinese landscape architect.

blocks.title: Confucius statue and the wisdom walk

children.text: A life-size granite statue of Confucius stands in the garden. According to the park authority (NPDC), it is said to have been donated by the Anvil Business Club in return for China's support of the Rizal Monument in Siong-que, Jinjiang City, Fujian, and it honors teachers and promotes Confucian and Filipino values. Along the nearby 'wisdom walk', Chinese proverbs are shown in Chinese characters with English and Filipino translations, which makes for a pleasant slow stroll.

blocks.title: Stone lanterns, pond and bridge of the Japanese Garden

children.text: The Japanese Garden combines trees, ornamental plants, stone lanterns, a lagoon and Japanese-style bridges. Its colors are quieter and its lines tidier than those of the Chinese Garden, so within one park you can compare the garden aesthetics of the two countries right away. The basic route is to cross the bridge and circle the edge of the pond.

blocks.title: The story of the Japanese gift

children.text: According to the NPDC, First Lady Imelda Marcos asked the Japanese Embassy in the Philippines for a Japanese garden starting in 1967, and President Marcos made the same request to Japanese Prime Minister Eisaku Sato. At Sato's request, Japanese companies and organizations raised more than
and Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs added
. The finished garden was turned over on June 11, 1969, with the Marcoses and former Prime Minister Nobusuke Kishi in attendance.

blocks.title: Marker for the 13 Martyrs of Bagumbayan

children.text: Inside the Japanese Garden stands the Trece Martires de Bagumbayan marker. It honors 13 Filipino patriots who were executed by the Spanish authorities on January 11, 1897, after being accused of treason and sedition following the revolution that began in 1896. It is an unusual place where the memory of friendship with Japan and the Philippine independence movement meet in the middle of a garden.

According to the NPDC's usage guide, casual personal photo and video shoots, vlogs themed on tourism or the park, and simple gatherings with no setup are free. Pre-nuptial, birthday and anniversary shoots and commercial shoots are listed separately as small activities and may need a permit and a fee (the published rates cover venue rental only), so if you plan to bring a tripod and lights, ask the NPDC in advance.

blocks.title: Linking up with the rest of the park

children.text: The two gardens are in the same park as the Rizal Monument, the light and sound show and the National Museum complex, so they are easy to combine into a one-day route. After resting in the gardens, continue to the nearby Orchidarium and Butterfly Pavilion, the National Museum and Intramuros to fill a satisfying half day in central Manila.

items.title: Half-day walk
items.subtitle: The two gardens and a loop of the park

children.text: Get off at United Nations Avenue station on LRT-1 and walk about
5 minutes
to the Rizal Park entrance. The sun is still gentle, which makes this the best time to walk the whole park.
From the central lawn, head toward the Chinese Garden, see the dragon gate, and look around the pavilions, the pond, the Confucius statue and the wisdom walk.
Pass the old Planetarium building and move on to the Japanese Garden. See the stone lanterns, pond and bridge, and read the text in front of the 13 Martyrs marker.
Look around the nearby Orchidarium and Butterfly Pavilion. There may be an entrance fee, so check the sign.
Take a quick look at the National Museum area, then have lunch at a restaurant across from the park or in Intramuros.
The gardens themselves take only
1–2 hours
, so a common plan is the gardens in the morning and Intramuros in the afternoon.

items.title: Sunset route
items.subtitle: A garden walk followed by sunset and the fountain

children.text: Enter the park and walk through the Chinese Garden and then the Japanese Garden. The afternoon light slants across the pavilions and ponds, which makes for good photos.
Walk toward Manila Bay to watch the sunset. The time the sun starts to set changes with the season, so check that day's time.
Finish before the park closes, head out to a bright main road, and take a Grab or taxi. Inside the park, it is safer to leave early once the sun goes down.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), a Grab or airport taxi to Rizal Park usually takes
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
, depending heavily on traffic.
Approaching the park from Roxas Boulevard is said to offer plenty of parking and less congestion than Taft Avenue.
Get off at United Nations Avenue station on LRT-1 and it is about
5 minutes
on foot to the park entrance. From Central Terminal station it is also a
5–10 minutes
walk.
The fare is around
depending on the distance. Check the latest fare table.
Take a jeepney along Taft Avenue or T.M. Kalaw Avenue and get off near Luneta. The base fare is about
A Grab from Makati is listed at roughly

. It varies with the time of day and traffic.
The gardens are in the central section of the park, so there is a walk from the entrance. Searching for 'Rizal Park Chinese Garden' in Google Maps makes it easier to find the way.

The dry season from November to May is the best time for walking. December to February in particular is relatively cool and clear, and the pavilions photograph well. The gardens are mostly outdoors, so the midday sun is strong.
Early morning and late afternoon are the best times of day. Around 7 a.m. the air is cool and many local joggers are out, and around 5:30 p.m. the light is soft.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Best season for walks and photos; crowded on weekends and holidays
Walk in the morning or at sunset, and bring water and a hat
Bring an umbrella, and adjust outdoor plans if a typhoon is forecast

The gardens are close to Ermita and Malate in Manila, so if you stay nearby you can get around on foot. The old Manila Hotel stands across from the park, and Malate and Ermita have many mid-range hotels and hostels. Lodging and prices vary a lot by season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

Picnics on a spread mat are said to be prohibited inside the park. Buy snacks and drinks from stalls around the park, and for a proper meal it is easier to use the restaurant areas of Intramuros, Ermita or Malate. Korean restaurants are also easy to find in Malate and Ermita.
The gardens are small, so plan a one-day itinerary that combines them with the Rizal Monument, the National Museum and Intramuros.
Admission fees and opening hours differ from guide to guide. Check at the entrance and keep small change of ₱10–50 ready.
The park as a whole is described as usually open from 5 a.m. to 9 p.m., but the gardens may close earlier, so leave some margin in an afternoon plan.
The 13 Martyrs marker in the Japanese Garden and the wisdom walk in the Chinese Garden take time to read. English translations are included, so they are worth reading slowly.
Many sections have little shade, so water, a hat and sunscreen are essential. Bring a small umbrella in case of rain.
Shoots with a tripod or lights, and wedding shoots, may need a permit and a fee, so ask the NPDC (02 8541-8296 or other official contacts) in advance.
Starting and ending your Manila trip at the park cuts down on walking. Plan your route around United Nations Avenue station on LRT-1.
Admission fees and opening hours differ by source and must be checked on site, and pickpocketing is reported around the edges of the park after dark.
Phone snatching is reported on the Taft Avenue edge after dark. Late in the day, do not walk to the LRT; call a Grab from the park entrance.
If a fee for admission or filming is collected at the garden entrance, pay at the official counter and get a receipt.
Parts of the gardens can be closed for events, shoots or rentals. The Chinese Garden is rented out as an event venue for up to 150 guests, so check before you visit.
The pond edges and bridge railings are slippery after rain. Wear shoes with good grip rather than sandals.
There are no-eating zones inside the park. Take your trash with you.
Manila's flagship urban park, with the Rizal Monument, the light and sound show and a big lawn. The gardens are inside this park, so no separate trip is needed.
The National Museum complex in the northeast of the park can be reached on foot from the gardens. Check opening hours and closing days before you go.
The walled city of the Spanish colonial era, reached north of the park on foot or by jeepney. Gardens in the morning and a walk along the walls in the afternoon is a common pairing.
A marine theme park on the Manila Bay side to the west of the park, a good stop with children after visiting the gardens.
